MaveMD currently contains 476,076 variant effect measurements spanning 39 disease-associated genes, enabling classification of 75% of VUS. MaveMD supports future data generation efforts and the use of MAVE evidence in clinical practice, reducing VUS burden and improving outcomes.

title: DrugSAGE: a transcriptome aggregation approach using cell lines for drug response imputation
abstract: Abstract Accurate prediction of drug response is critical for optimizing the clinical application of cancer therapies. Nevertheless, owing to genetic and genomic heterogeneity and the complex tumor microenvironment, cancer samples may exhibit heterogeneous responses to the same therapeutic agents, even when harboring identical driver mutations or genes. In this study, we developed DrugSAGE, a novel framework that leverages Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to model cellular heterogeneity and accurately predict drug response from transcriptomic data. DrugSAGE enhances prediction by aggregating features from a sample and its most similar counterparts. Critically, we introduce a customized linear layer incorporating gene-pathway annotations to provide biological interpretability, facilitating the identification of key pathways driving the prediction. We benchmarked DrugSAGE using TCGA bulk data, six public bulk datasets, and four scRNA-seq datasets. Predictions from DrugSAGE showed significant associations between drugs and their known target genes (e.g., HER2 + inhibitors, MET inhibitors, BRAF inhibitors) or significant differences between patient groups stratified by their treatments (e.g., Erlotinib, PLX4720, 5-Fluorouracil). Furthermore, we show DrugSAGE can effectively predict drug response at the single-cell level. Additionally, by analyzing pathway-based embeddings, we identified pathways crucial to the models, including those involved in cancer, MAPK signaling, endocytosis, and JAK-STAT signaling, among others. Compared to previous methods, DrugSAGE demonstrated superior or comparable performance, offering a novel approach for predicting drug responses.

title: Genome-wide meQTL mapping reveals genetic control of DNA methylation in colon cancer
abstract: Methylation quantitative trait loci (meQTLs) are essential for understanding the role of DNA methylation in the genetic susceptibility to colorectal cancer (CRC). However, studies of meQTLs in East Asians and at single base-pair resolution are relatively scarce. This study aims to characterize the genetic regulation of global DNA methylation and explore the underlying mechanisms of meQTLs contributing to CRC risk. To address this problem, we recruited 250 patients with colon cancer between 2007 and 2018 and isolated colon tumor samples with matched adjacent normal tissues. We conducted multi-omics profiling using whole-genome sequencing, whole-genome bisulfite sequencing, and RNA sequencing. Our analysis included methylome and transcriptome correlations (eQTMs) and local genetic regulation (meQTLs and eQTLs). To investigate the genetic impact of meQTLs on colon cancer, we systematically performed functional annotations, co-localization analyses, and mediation analyses. We identified a total of 48,429,542 cis-acting SNP-CpG associations in 553,834 meCpGs throughout the genome ( p < 2 × 10 −12 ). 63% of these CpGs linked to multiple lead meQTLs, suggesting pleiotropic genetic regulation of methylation. 16.8% of lead meQTLs were situated within the differentially methylated regions (DMRs) between tumoral and normal tissues, indicating that meQTLs may influence dysregulated methylation sites. Colocalization analysis revealed 14,104 CpG-Gene pairs that were likely to share causal variants, with meQTLs mediating 51% of the SNP effects on gene expression. Pathway analysis uncovered epigenetic regulation of translation, RNA polymerase, and DNA repair signaling pathways. Furthermore, our findings covered 86.6% of the previously identified CRC GWAS risk loci, and 40% of them were significantly co-localized. This study provides a comprehensive resource that comprises integrative genetic, epigenomic, and transcriptomic datasets on colon cancer, revealing co-regulation of methylation and gene expression at the single-base resolution across the genome, thereby enhancing the functional understanding of epigenetic and gene regulation underlying colon cancer.

title: Blood cell composition reveals distinct biological interpretation of DNA methylation age and age acceleration
abstract: BACKGROUND: Epigenetic clocks are widely applied biomarkers of biological age, but their biological underpinnings remain unclear. We previously showed that epigenetic clocks are affected by naïve and memory T cell proportions, suggesting blood cell composition as a potential driver. However, analysis of cell composition is complicated by collinearity between cell fractions. METHODS: We first develop a principal component analysis (PCA) method that is robust to collinearity of blood cell counts and show that this approach provides biologically meaningful insights. Next, we quantify the contribution of cell composition to DNA methylation age and age acceleration estimated by six 1st - or 2nd -generation epigenetic clocks in an analysis of 4,058 samples. Finally, we test the influence of cell composition on the association between age acceleration and 176 incident health outcomes using a study of 18,859 individuals. RESULTS: We find that up to 53% of the variation in DNA methylation age can be attributed to cell counts, with a particularly strong contribution of the balance between naïve and memory T cells. Associations between age acceleration and cell counts are weaker (up to 21% variance explained) and, for 2nd -generation clocks, primarily involve neutrophils. We validate the contribution of cell counts to epigenetic clocks using artificial cell mixtures. Interestingly, cell composition significantly attenuates the association of age acceleration investigated with 176 incident health outcomes, although this effect remains modest. CONCLUSIONS: DNAmAge and AgeAccel are markedly different in their associations with cell composition, indicating that they - at least in part - reflect different biological processes. Surprisingly, the variation in age acceleration that can be attributed to blood cell composition only has a minor contribution to its association with mortality and incident disease outcomes.

title: A nationwide prospective randomized trial for diagnosing developmental disorders demonstrates genome sequencing outperforms standard of care
abstract: BACKGROUND: Exome (ES) or genome (GS) sequencing are recommended as first- or second-tier molecular tests for patients with developmental disorders (DD), but the clinical utility of GS continues to be debated. METHODS: This prospective randomized trial involving all Belgian human genetics centers compared the standard of care (SoC) - combining ES and chromosomal microarray analysis or shallow GS - with GS for 567 individuals with unexplained DD. The study was retrospectively registered. RESULTS: The diagnostic yield of GS was 39.8% (113/284) vs. 30% for SoC (85/283) (p = 0.015), mainly due to an increased detection of single nucleotide variants and indels (+ 8.7%). GS also enabled the detection of three non-coding (potential) pathogenic variants. Across both study arms, the diagnostic yield was higher for females (45.5%, 97/213) compared to males (28.5%, 101/354) (p < 0.001). Upon correction for the sex distribution and analytical differences between the study arms, the diagnostic yield difference between GS and SoC was reduced to 7.3% (p = 0.069). De novo variants were found for 23.6% of patients. Analysis of inherited variants in genes associated with autosomal dominant phenotypes contributed more to the diagnostic yield (3.9%) than X-linked variants (1.9%), and to a similar extent as autosomal recessive variants (4.1%). CONCLUSIONS: This nationwide study indicates GS outperforms SoC for the diagnosis of patients with DD in a decentralized hospital setting and well-characterized cohort. The results also highlight the importance of evaluating autosomal dominant inherited variants in genomics analyses for DD. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07051213, 03-07-2025).

title: Deconstructing cervical cancer heterogeneity: squamous cell carcinoma subtypes and CCM2 vulnerability in adenocarcinoma
abstract: Cervical cancer, a leading female malignancy with marked histological heterogeneity, encompassing squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), adenocarcinoma (AC), adenosquamous carcinoma (ASC), and neuroendocrine carcinoma (NEC), which differ in prognosis and treatment response. However, the molecular features of these histotypes, particularly the rare ASC and NEC subtypes, remain incompletely understood, and a dedicated molecular classification for SCC is lacking, limiting the development of subtype-specific therapeutic strategies. We performed deep proteomic profiling of 404 cervical cancer tissue samples, comprising 298 SCC, 74 AC, 22 ASC, and 10 NEC cases. Comparative proteomic, pathway enrichment, tumor microenvironment, survival, and machine-learning analyses were conducted to characterize subtype-specific molecular features, identify candidate therapeutic targets, and develop a prognostically relevant molecular classification system for SCC. Distinct proteomic signatures were observed between SCC and AC. AC was characterized by activation of epithelial-mesenchymal transition and glycoprotein metabolic pathways, and CCM2 was functionally validated as a candidate mediator of AC cell invasion and migration. SCC was classified into three cervical squamous molecular subtypes (CSMSs): CSMS1 (immunosuppressive), CSMS2 (immune-enriched), and CSMS3 (oxidative stress response). This classification significantly stratified patient survival in an independent external cohort (log-rank p = 0.022). Clinical-molecular subtype analysis showed the CSMS1 subtype had the poorest prognosis in specific subgroups (age > 45, BMI < 25 kg/m 2 , moderate differentiation, FIGO III/IV), especially with non-surgical treatment, supporting “clinical + molecular” stratification for high-risk identification. This large-scale proteomic study provides a comprehensive molecular landscape of the major histotypes of cervical cancer, identifies CCM2 as a potential therapeutic target associated with the aggressive phenotype of AC, and establishes a clinically relevant molecular classification system for SCC. Integrating the CSMS classification with conventional clinical characteristics may improve the identification of high-risk patients and facilitate precision management of cervical cancer.

title: ACSS2-dependent histone lactylation amplifies ferroptotic injury via a metabolic feedback loop in ulcerative colitis
abstract: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is marked by profound metabolic reprogramming and intestinal epithelial barrier breakdown. However, how altered cellular metabolism contributes to epithelial injury remains incompletely understood. Recent evidence suggests that metabolic intermediates can drive epigenetic modifications, but their role in regulating ferroptosis in UC has not been fully elucidated. We integrated transcriptomic profiling of UC patient biopsies, dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)–induced mouse colitis models, and in vitro stimulation of intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) to explore the metabolic/epigenetic/ferroptosis axis. Histone lactylation was assessed via CUT&Tag and immunodetection. Functional studies employed intestinal epithelium-specific Acss2 knockout mice and a butyrate-modified lipid nanoparticle (BLNP) system for targeted delivery of ACSS2 siRNA. Pharmacological inhibition of c-Myc, a common upstream transcriptional activator, was also evaluated. Human UC tissues and DSS-treated mice showed a glycolytic shift with elevated HK2 expression and lactate accumulation. Lactate was converted by ACSS2 into lactyl-CoA, promoting histone H3K18 lactylation (H3K18la). This modification upregulated HK2, ACSS2, and ACSL4, establishing a lactate-responsive feedback program that increased epithelial susceptibility to lipid peroxidation and ferroptotic injury. Increased ferroptotic markers coincided with tight junction disruption in UC models. Genetic ablation of Acss2 or c-Myc inhibition dampened H3K18la, reduced ACSL4 expression, and preserved IEC viability. Moreover, systemic administration of ACSS2 siRNA via BLNPs effectively reversed colitis pathology, restored tight junction integrity, and reduced ferroptotic injury, without overt toxicity. Our findings identify a lactate-fueled ACSS2/H3K18la-associated feedback program as an amplifier of ferroptosis-prone epithelial injury in UC. Targeting this axis represents a promising therapeutic strategy to restore mucosal homeostasis. These results highlight ACSS2 as a mechanistic and translationally relevant target in inflammatory bowel disease.

title: MOSAIC: Intra-tumoral heterogeneity characterization through large-scale spatial and cell-resolved multi-omics profiling
abstract: Abstract Precision oncology remains challenging due to gaps in understanding tumor biology and immunology, as well as the scarcity of consistent data across large cohorts. Here, we introduce MOSAIC (Multi-Omics Spatial Atlas in Cancer), a multi-center clinical Omics study designed to systematically profile thousands of cancer samples, with a focus on spatial and single-cell data across multiple tumor types. MOSAIC exploits recent technological advances to integrate spatial and single-cell data with complementary data modalities, including hematoxylin-eosin histology scans, bulk RNA and exome sequences, to generate comprehensive representations of cancer histology, genomics, and transcriptomics. MOSAIC also collects extensive and curated clinical information to ensure that patients meet the precise inclusion criteria for each cohort. The consortium aims to integrate all data modalities using artificial intelligence and other computational approaches in order to identify clinically-relevant biomarkers and cancer subtypes. This paper outlines the core objectives of MOSAIC, its potential impact, early proofs-of-concept, design, and experimental considerations. Additionally, we introduce the MOSAIC Window initiative, featuring the first released dataset from 60 patients, offering a glimpse into the project’s groundbreaking potential. Using four selected patients, we demonstrate the power of multi-omic approaches to analyze and interpret intra-tumoral variability within and across patients, providing insights on specific drug sensitivity of cancer subpopulations and revealing potential impacts on therapeutic recommendations.

title: Proteomic risk scores facilitate early prediction of cardiometabolic diseases in pre-clinical obesity
abstract: Obesity is a major risk factor for cardiometabolic diseases, but individuals with obesity differ substantially in their future disease trajectories. We aimed to evaluate whether circulating proteins provide incremental and biologically interpretable risk information for incident type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia among individuals with an operationally defined pre-clinical obesity phenotype in UK Biobank. Among 13,931 UK Biobank participants with abnormal adiposity but without established obesity-related diseases at baseline, 2,919 circulating proteins were analyzed. Single-protein associations with incident type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia were assessed using Cox proportional hazards models. Protein-based risk scores (ProteinScores) were developed using elastic-net Cox regression for 5-, 10-, and 15-year prediction horizons. Predictive performance was evaluated using AUC, calibration, and category-based net reclassification improvement, and compared with baseline covariate models, extended clinical models, available UK Biobank polygenic risk scores, and metabolomic scores. Pathway enrichment analyses were performed to characterize the biological processes represented by ProteinScore proteins. We identified 973 Bonferroni-significant protein–disease associations involving 653 unique proteins across the three cardiometabolic outcomes. ProteinScores improved discrimination beyond age- and sex-adjusted and baseline covariate models across prediction horizons. Compared with extended clinical models that included disease-specific clinical indicators, incremental improvement was more outcome- and horizon-dependent, with significant AUC gains observed for selected longer-term predictions. Calibration and reclassification analyses showed that ProteinScores provided additional risk-stratification information in several disease–horizon combinations, although the magnitude of improvement varied. ProteinScores showed favorable performance compared with available PRS fields and MetaboScores in this UK Biobank framework, but the relative performance differed by outcome and prediction horizon. Pathway analyses implicated lipid transport, lipoprotein remodeling, extracellular matrix organization, peptide hormone processing, and immune-inflammatory signaling. Plasma proteomic profiling provides effective risk stratification for future cardiometabolic diseases in individuals with pre-clinical obesity. These findings highlight the potential of integrating dynamic proteomic signatures into early clinical frameworks to advance precision prevention strategies in obesity management.

title: Integration of single cell omics with biobank data discovers allele-specific trans effects of SREBF1 on adipocyte expression of nearly 100 genes
abstract: Abstract Background Given the high global prevalence of obesity and lack of mechanistic, cell-type level knowledge of regulatory genes predisposing obesity, it would be critical to improve our understanding of how gene expression profiles are regulated in trans in adipocytes, the main cell-type in subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT), and how that relates to obesity. Methods We utilize single nucleus RNA-sequencing data sets from human SAT biopsies to elucidate the heritability of cardiometabolic disease risk in SAT cell-types and identify transcription factor (TF) encoding genes present in multiple functional pathways of the SAT cell-type marker genes. We integrate genome-wide association study (GWAS) data with expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) data and conduct polygenic risk analyses for abdominal obesity and type 2 diabetes (T2D) to test if a cis regulatory GWAS variant for a key TF encoding gene, SREBF1 , harbors allele-specific trans effects on adipocyte marker genes and their polygenic risk. Results We show that the heritability of epigenetic sites around SAT adipocyte marker genes is enriched for abdominal obesity, and that these cell-type markers are also enriched for central pathways of adipocyte function. Next, we discover SREBF1 as the most frequent TF in these adipocyte pathways and identify rs8079321, an abdominal obesity and T2D GWAS variant, regulating the bulk SAT SREBF1 expression in cis . We further discover and verify in an independent SAT snRNA-seq cohort, that the GWAS risk allele of rs8079321 affects the adipocyte expression of SREBF1 in cis and 89 SAT adipocyte marker genes in trans . Finally, we demonstrate that this trans effect extends to the polygenic risk by showing that the partitioned abdominal obesity and T2D polygenic risk scores of the 89 trans genes differ by the risk allele of rs8079321 in the UK Biobank, indicating widespread cell-type level cis -mediated trans effects on highly common CMDs. Conclusions We discover that the SAT master TF, SREBF1, trans regulates the adipocyte expression profiles of nearly one hundred adipocyte marker genes in an allele-specific way, a finding that indicates that human trans -eQTL genes can be identified by integrating single cell omics with biobank data.

title: MAC-explorer: bridging genome-based taxonomy and an identification tool for the Mycobacterium avium complex
abstract: The Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) comprises genetically close nontuberculous mycobacteria responsible for human and animal infections worldwide. Increasing availability of whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data offers new opportunities for genomic surveillance and lineage tracking of these pathogens. However, the taxonomy of the MAC remains unstable, with inconsistent species and subspecies boundaries that hinder reproducible genome-based identification complicating diagnostics and antimicrobial management. Furthermore, a major barrier to the clinical and epidemiological integration of WGS is the current lack of standardized, accessible identification tools capable of translating complex genomic similarity into harmonized taxonomic assignments. We performed a comprehensive in silico analysis of 2,737 MAC genomes using pairwise average nucleotide identity (ANI). Species and subspecies boundaries were statistically modeled at 95% and 98% ANI thresholds. A consensus genome-based framework combining FastANI and dRep clustering was developed. Machine learning classifiers based on k-mer frequency profiles were trained to reproduce genomic delineations. Fifteen species-level clusters were identified, with 99.9% concordance to GTDB-Tk reference classifications. Within M. avium , subsp. avium , subsp. hominissuis , and subsp. silvaticum formed a single genomic continuum, while the IS900-positive M. avium subsp. avium lineage paratuberculosis remained distinct but did not reach subspecies level divergence. Within M. intracellulare , subsp. chimaera showed deep internal structure, supporting recognition of M. intracellulare subsp. yongonense , whereas genomes assigned to M. paraintracellulare clustered within M. intracellulare subsp. intracellulare . Several nominal species ( M. bouchedurhonense , M. timonense ) lacked genomic coherence. The MAC displayed an open pangenome (191,904 gene clusters; 0.8% universal core). Machine learning classifiers trained on k-mer frequency profiles accurately reproduced whole-genome delineations, achieving near-perfect performances (Cohen’s kappa = 0.994). We provide a standardized, genome-based framework for classification of the MAC and implement it in MAC-Explorer (https://mycobacteriaexplorer.fr), an open-access web tool for automated MAC identification. By integrating k-mer -based classification and insertion sequence screening, MAC-Explorer delivers reproducible and harmonized species- and lineage-level assignments, providing a robust foundation for genome-based identification and lineage tracking of MAC isolates.

title: Senescent cancer-associated fibroblasts secrete Tenascin-C to promote tumor progression in high-grade serous ovarian cancer
abstract: Cellular senescence is a hallmark of cancer, and senescent cancer-associated fibroblasts (seneCAFs) contribute to tumor progression across multiple malignancies. However, how seneCAFs promote high-grade serous ovarian (HGSOC) remains unclear. We integrated public single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), spatial transcriptomic data, and clinical specimens to characterize seneCAFs and define their transcriptomic signature. A prognostic model based on the seneCAFs signature was developed using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO)-based machine learning to predict survival outcomes. Cell-cell communication analysis was performed to identify candidate seneCAFs-derived effectors. In vitro and in vivo functional assays were conducted to investigate the pro-tumorigenic role of seneCAFs and the regulatory mechanisms governing the expression of key effector. Furthermore, pan-cancer analysis was carried out to evaluate the prognostic value of the seneCAFs risk model and the candidate effector across multiple cancer types. CAFs in HGSOC exhibited elevated cellular senescence, and the seneCAFs-based risk model predicted poor survival. Among its prognostic genes, Tenascin-C (TNC) emerged as a key seneCAFs-secreted effector that signals to tumor cells. Functional assays confirmed that seneCAFs-derived TNC promoted HGSOC progression. Mechanistically, TNC activated SDC4-ERK signaling in tumor cells to induce epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), while NF-κB activation in seneCAFs transcriptionally upregulated TNC expression. Pan-cancer analysis linked high seneCAFs risk score and TNC expression to worse overall survival. The seneCAFs transcriptomic signature and its risk model stratify HGSOC patients and predict worse clinical outcomes. Our study offers a novel insight about seneCAFs promote tumor progression and identifies TNC as a potential therapeutic target for HGSOC and other solid tumors.

title: Emergence of locally transmitting and drug-resistant clones shapes global expansion of Mycobacterium tuberculosis Lineage 3
abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis Lineage 3 (L3) is one of the major human-adapted MTBC lineages and is highly prevalent in parts of South Asia, East Africa, and Central Asia, although it remains less well characterized than other lineages. In particular, its capacity for sustained transmission and adaptation outside historically endemic regions remains unclear. We analyzed 7,472 publicly available L3 genomes from 38 countries within a global dataset of ~ 90,000 M. tuberculosis genomes. Population structure was resolved using phylogenetic reconstruction and hierarchical Bayesian clustering. Phylogeographic and phylodynamic analyses inferred dispersal history and demographic dynamics. Transmission patterns were assessed using genomic clustering, terminal branch lengths, and time-scaled haplotypic density (THD). Genome-wide scans identified signatures of positive selection and drug-resistance mutations. The dominant L3.1.1 clade (> 95% of L3 isolates) was resolved into six monophyletic sublineages (L3.1.1.1–L3.1.1.6) with distinct geographic distributions and demographic trajectories. Phylogeographic reconstruction indicated South Asia as the probable origin for most sublineages, followed by multiple intercontinental dispersal events. While many European isolates were associated with migration, genomic clustering identified 1,399 isolates consistent with potential local transmission, and sublineage-resolved selection analyses highlighted Rv1500 as consistently enriched in European local clusters. Phylodynamic analyses revealed recent expansion in L3.1.1.1, L3.1.1.5, and L3.1.1.6. Overall, 29.8% of isolates carried resistance-associated mutations, with L3.1.1.6 showing the highest burden (45.4%) and enrichment for pre-extensively drug-resistant strains. Within this sublineage, compensatory mutations in rpoA and rpoC were associated with elevated THD, indicating a potential role in restoring fitness and facilitating the spread of highly resistant clones. These findings reveal previously unrecognized diversity and heterogeneous evolutionary trajectories within L3. While global dissemination is largely driven by migration, certain sublineages exhibit patterns consistent with local amplification and expansion beyond their historical range. The emergence of highly drug-resistant and potentially transmissible clones, exemplified by L3.1.1.6, underscores the importance of sublineage–resolved genomic surveillance for TB control.

title: Survival and causes of death in primary mitochondrial diseases
abstract: Abstract Background Primary mitochondrial diseases affect 1 in 4300 livebirths and cause early death or lifelong disability but our understanding of their impact on survival and causes of death is limited. There is conflicting evidence about whether they cause an increased incidence of cancer. We aimed to determine survival, causes of death and risk of developing cancer in people with mitochondrial disease by linking genetic results with routinely collected healthcare data at a national scale. Methods Individuals with mitochondrial diseases were identified in England (population 60.2 million) by National Health Service diagnostic laboratories and Genomics England. A curated cohort was assembled. Individual consent was not required because the National Disease Registration Service has legal permission to collect patient data. We used national datasets to find out the vital status, cause of death and any cancer diagnoses for each individual. Kaplan-Meier survival, Cox regression model and standardised cancer incidence ratio were analysed. Results 1266 unique individuals were identified, with 1164 having a known region in England. Following clinical review, 1107 were included (527 males, 580 females, median age 48 years, age range from infancy to 90 years). 74% had a mitochondrial DNA diagnosis and 26% had nuclear genetic diagnosis. 170 were deceased. 159 were diagnosed during childhood (14.3%). Most childhood deaths were due to the underlying mitochondrial disorder. Common causes of death in adults included cardiac, cancers, and pneumonia. Survival after diagnosis varied by genetic diagnosis and by age at diagnosis with poorer survival for people diagnosed during childhood (hazard ratio 2.11, p < 0.001) or older age (2.83, p < 0.001) and those with recessive POLG disease (hazard ratio 3.06, p < 0.001). For the whole cohort, survival at 10 years after genetic diagnosis was 80.3% (95% confidence interval 76.9% to 83.7%) and survival at 20 years after diagnosis was 58.9% (95% confidence interval 49.6% to 70.0%). Standardised cancer incidence ratios did not show a difference in cancer incidence compared to the general population. Conclusions Survival was much longer than anticipated, with differences due to the precise genetic diagnosis and age at onset. Despite prior contradictory evidence, there was no increased cancer risk in this large cohort.

title: Early NOTCH1 mutation is positively selected but epistatically suppresses evolution of later esophageal squamous-cell carcinoma drivers
abstract: Abstract Background Somatic mutations commonly accumulate in histologically normal tissues and contribute to cancer development. However, many mutations that are common in normal tissue are also found in cancers from the same organ, making their role in malignant progression unclear. To address this, we asked whether such mutations increase cell proliferation and survival to different degrees at different steps of esophageal tumor development, and whether they alter selection for other driver mutations. Methods We used a quantitative evolutionary framework to distinguish underlying mutation rate from selection across two steps of esophageal development: from organogenesis to clonal histologically normal esophageal epithelium, and from that tissue to esophageal squamous-cell carcinoma. Analyzing sequence data from 2171 samples, we estimated step-specific selection on recurrent somatic mutations, corresponding to increased cellular division and survival, and tested whether mutations in one gene earlier in the trajectory changed selection for mutations on another. We additionally examined somatic copy-number alterations and single-cell transcriptomic profiles to contextualize these evolutionary patterns within broader genomic and cellular changes during progression. Results NOTCH1 mutations were strongly selected during the clonal expansion of histologically normal esophageal epithelium, explaining their high prevalence in that tissue. However, for the first time, we show that there is little to no positive selection for NOTCH1, NOTCH2, and FAT1 mutations during progression from clonal histologically normal esophageal tissue to esophageal squamous-cell carcinoma in humans, leading to a conclusion that these alterations promote clonal expansion in normal tissue, but do not drive malignant progression from established normal clones. Moreover, we provide a somatic genetic basis for this step-specific effect: we demonstrate for the first time that mutations in NOTCH1 exhibit antagonistic epistasis with mutations of TP53 and RB1 , reducing selection for these key tumor suppressor alterations during tumor development. Consistent with this model, copy-number alterations associated with later ESCC progression were more strongly selected in TP53 -mutant samples, supporting the idea that TP53 disruption promotes a genomic context more permissive for malignant evolution. Conclusions Early somatic mutations can promote clonal expansion in normal tissue without promoting cancer, and in some cases may limit progression by reducing selection for later driver events. NOTCH1 and other genes can shape evolutionary trajectories in ways that ultimately constrain malignant progression. By separating mutation rate from selection, quantifying step-specific genetic interactions, and considering broader changes in genomic and cellular context, our study shows that the effects of recurrent mutations depend strongly on disease stage and mutational context—what promotes clonal expansion in normal tissue may later impede growth or survival in tumors. These insights underscore the need for precision strategies that account for the shifting fitness landscape across premalignant and malignant stages, informing early detection, prevention, and therapeutic prioritization.

title: Decoding coupled epigenetic-fragmentomic signals in circulating cell-free DNA for interpretable cancer diagnosis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Plasma cell-free DNA (cfDNA) whole-genome methylation sequencing enables simultaneous characterization of DNA methylation and fragmentomic features for cancer detection. However, it remains unclear whether methylation library preparation faithfully preserves fragmentomic signals, how methylation and fragmentation are biologically coupled, and how these two modalities can be systematically integrated. METHODS: We systematically evaluated the preservation of cfDNA fragmentomic features in whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) and enzymatic methyl sequencing (EM-seq) relative to conventional whole-genome sequencing (WGS). We next investigated the biological relationship between methylation and fragmentation and delineated methylation haplotype blocks (MHBs) directly from plasma cfDNA as biologically interpretable units for organizing multimodal cfDNA signals. Guided by these findings, we developed multimodal diagnostic models integrating complementary methylation and fragmentomic features. RESULTS: Canonical cfDNA fragmentomic patterns were partially preserved across methylation sequencing protocols, although the degree of preservation varied among individual features. DNA methylation levels were associated with characteristic fragment length and end-motif patterns. Plasma-derived MHBs exhibited tissue-associated regulatory features and distinct patterns of chromatin accessibility, repeat enrichment, and methylation heterogeneity, providing biologically interpretable units for integrated cfDNA analysis. Within these regions, methylation and fragmentomic signals exhibited coordinated yet complementary patterns. Leveraging this framework, we developed Fragmentomics And Methylation Ensemble (FAME), an interpretable multimodal model integrating MHB-centered methylation and fragmentomic features for cancer detection and tissue-of-origin prediction, and further extended it with complementary genome-wide methylation and fragmentomic features to generate a genome-wide-augmented FAME model (FAME-GW). Across cross-validation, independent validation, and comparisons with THEMIS (THorough Epigenetic Marker Integration Solution), SPOT-MAS (screening for the presence of tumor by methylation and size), and DELFI (DNA evaluation of fragments for early interception), FAME-based models achieved robust diagnostic performance, with FAME providing a compact and interpretable representation and FAME-GW delivering the strongest overall predictive performance. CONCLUSIONS: Our study demonstrates that cfDNA whole-genome methylation sequencing partially preserves informative fragmentomic signals and establishes plasma-derived MHBs as biologically interpretable units for organizing and integrating complementary methylation and fragmentomic information. This framework provides insight into the coupling of epigenetic and fragmentomic information and an effective strategy for interpretable cfDNA-based cancer diagnosis.

title: Variant classification challenges in genes associated with multiple disorders contribute to the persistent interlaboratory discordance
abstract: Abstract Background Accurate germline variant classification requires correct application of ACMG/AMP evidence criteria and assignment of pathogenicity to a specific disease entity and mode of inheritance. Whether laboratories apply this disease-specific approach consistently to genes associated with multiple disorders remains insufficiently characterized. Methods We conducted a national interlaboratory study of germline variant classification using a proficiency-testing dataset comprising 13 variants across five clinical scenarios from 128 Chinese clinical genetic laboratories. Results Overall concordance was achieved for 6 of 13 variants, whereas 7 showed clinically meaningful cross-category discordance. Residual disagreement was partly attributable to omission or inappropriate use of ACMG/AMP evidence criteria, inconsistent strength assignment, and disease-context-specific interpretation. A prominent pattern of discordance involved disease-specific interpretation of variants in genes associated with multiple disorders. For variants in APOB , LZTR1 , MYH7 , and EPCAM , laboratories frequently transferred pathogenic assertions across disorders without adequately considering disease mechanism, inheritance pattern, or disorder-specific validity. By contrast, two GJB2 variants showed substantially higher categorical concordance. These errors could alter downstream clinical interpretation and, in some cases, implied management recommendations. Conclusions Disease-specific classification in multi-disease genes remains an important source of residual discordance despite improved criterion-level harmonization. Harmonization efforts should therefore extend beyond gene-level pathogenicity assessment toward mechanism-aware, disease-anchored classification frameworks and reporting practices. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

title: Charting brain structure in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome with clinical neuroimaging
authors: the ENIGMA 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome Working Group
abstract: Abstract Background 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22q11DS) is a common microdeletion associated with widespread brain alterations and elevated risk for schizophrenia and other neuropsychiatric conditions. Prospective research studies often exclude individuals with severe cognitive impairment, medical comorbidities, or inability to tolerate research magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) without sedation, features common in 22q11DS and other rare genetic disorders. This limits both the generalizability of neuroimaging findings and our understanding of the full phenotypic spectrum. Moreover, while standard brain growth charts quantify deviation from typical development, they cannot identify patients who are disproportionately affected relative to their genetic peers, limiting clinical utility for risk stratification. Leveraging clinical MRI data offers a scalable approach to address these gaps. Methods In this retrospective, cross-sectional study, we analyzed 92 patients with 22q11DS (age 0.5–21 years, 49% female) and 252 matched clinical controls. Using normative modeling derived from 1,995 reference clinical scans, we quantified patient brain deviations from population norms. We validated clinical findings against the independent ENIGMA-22q research consortium, characterized rates of extreme structural deviations to assess within-syndrome heterogeneity, correlated spatial patterns of brain alterations with gene expression from the Allen Human Brain Atlas, and generated syndrome-specific growth charts to test whether deviations from syndrome-specific norms predicted cognitive and language outcomes. Results Patients with 22q11DS showed widespread reductions in brain volumes (max Cohen’s d = −1.31) and cortical surface area (d = −0.71) with increased cortical thickness (d = 0.39). These findings were highly convergent with the ENIGMA-22q research cohort ( r = 0.61–0.87). Forty percent of patients showed at least one global brain measure below the 2.5th centile. Spatial patterns of cortical volume and surface area correlated with expression of genes within the 22q11.2 locus. In exploratory analyses, syndrome-specific growth chart deviations in cerebellar volumes relative to 22q11DS peers were nominally associated with lower language scores across two independent assessment methods ( p < 0.03), suggesting potential prognostic utility. Conclusions This study provides a critical proof of principle for using heterogeneous clinical imaging to robustly characterize brain structure in rare genetic disorders. Syndrome-specific growth charts provide a novel framework to quantify within-syndrome variability and demonstrate potential prognostic value by linking individual brain structure to cognitive outcomes.

title: Longitudinal single-cell and spatial profiling of sonic hedgehog medulloblastoma identifies novel therapeutic targets
abstract: Abstract Background Sonic hedgehog (SHH) medulloblastoma (MB) accounts for approximately one-third of all MB cases, the most common malignant brain tumor in children. Despite therapy, SHH MB relapse is frequent and has a dismal prognosis. New treatments for recurrent SHH MB are needed; however, the molecular drivers of relapse are poorly understood. Methods We profiled 22 SHH MB specimens (16 primary and 6 recurrent), including four primary–recurrent patient pairs, using overlapping single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq; n = 16), single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin sequencing (snATAC-seq; n = 13), and spatial transcriptomic ( n = 6) cohorts. We integrated these data with exome-derived variant calls from 25 specimens, including seven patients with primary and recurrent samples. Bulk RNA-seq data from 48 specimens representing 24 primary–recurrent pairs were used for validation. Results Our analyses show evidence of positive selection for nonsynonymous tumor mutations, including TP53 mutations involving its DNA-binding and tetramerization domains. TP53 mutations were associated with reduced base-excision repair (BER) gene expression and accessibility of linked cis-regulatory regions. Recurrent tumors showed increased tumor mutational burden (TMB) and an endoplasmic-reticulum (ER) stress expression program associated with poorer survival. Angiogenic gene expression and inferred immunosuppressive myeloid signaling were increased in recurrent disease. Conclusions These data define recurrence-associated cellular and regulatory programs, nominate candidate therapeutic targets and prognostic markers, and provide a single-cell and spatial atlas of SHH MB.

title: Development and validation of a trans‑ancestry polygenic risk score for coronary artery disease in the chinese population
abstract: Trans-ancestry polygenic risk scores (PRSs) have been proposed to address the limited transferability of European-specific PRSs to East Asian populations. However, their ability to improve risk prediction for coronary artery disease (CAD) in the Chinese population remains unclear. We aimed to develop and validate a trans-ancestry CAD PRS in the Chinese population by integrating European and East Asian genome-wide association studies (GWAS). Using summary statistics from large-scale CAD GWAS meta-analyses of East Asian and European populations, we constructed trans-ancestry PRSs via PRS-CSx in two configurations: PRS-meta, derived exclusively from GWAS results and linkage disequilibrium reference panels; and PRS-combine, optimized in a Chinese training set comprising 2,800 CAD cases and 2,055 controls. For comparison, we generated East Asian-specific PRSs using LDpred and pruning-and-thresholding methods, and additionally evaluated previously published CAD PRSs. The top-performing PRSs for each method in the training set were then externally validated in 72,782 individuals with genetic data from the China Kadoorie Biobank (CKB), a large-scale population-based cohort in China, with a mean follow-up of 12.1 years. In the training set, PRS-meta and PRS-combine exhibited comparable predictive performance, with odds ratios per standard deviation (SD) of 2.21 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.04, 2.38) and 2.23 (95% CI: 2.06, 2.41), respectively. Both trans-ancestry PRSs showed approximately 60% and 90% increases in pseudo-R 2 relative to the top-performing East Asian-specific and European-specific PRSs, respectively. In the CKB cohort, both scores were similarly associated with incident CAD, with hazard ratios (HRs) per SD of 1.33 (95% CI: 1.27, 1.41) for PRS-meta and 1.31 (95% CI: 1.24, 1.38) for PRS-combine. Individuals in the top versus bottom quintile had HRs of 2.06 (95% CI: 1.75, 2.42) for PRS-meta and 1.84 (95% CI: 1.56, 2.16) for PRS-combine. The trans-ancestry PRS constructed via PRS-CSx markedly improved CAD risk prediction in the Chinese population. This finding highlights an efficient and generalizable approach to developing more equitable PRSs for underrepresented populations, with PRS-meta demonstrating particular promise.

title: Combining MAVEs and computational predictors improves variant classification across ancestries in hereditary cancer genes
abstract: Abstract Many commonly used computational tools for variant effect prediction exhibit ancestry-related bias because they are trained on clinical or population datasets that under-represent global diversity, leading to uneven and sometimes unfair variant classification across ancestries. Multiplexed assays of variant effect (MAVEs) and population-free VEPs instead offer alternatives that are unbiased with respect to human ancestry, providing classification evidence that generalises across populations. Here, we evaluate MAVE- and VEP-based classification across five cancer-associated genes with high-quality MAVE datasets, focusing on three leading population-free VEPs: GEMME, EVE, and CPT-1. We find that MAVEs are more conservative and decisive in classification, assigning fewer variants to the pathogenic category while yielding fewer indeterminate classifications when calibrated to ACMG/AMP guidelines. While MAVEs show heightened sensitivity in functionally assayed regions, VEPs identify a broader range of pathogenic variants overall. By combining clinical evidence strengths from MAVEs and VEPs, we reclassify over 90% of variants of uncertain significance across the SG10K_Health and Mexico City Prospective Study reference datasets as at least likely benign or likely pathogenic. We further isolate variants where MAVE- and VEP-based classifications are discordant, highlighting method-specific limitations. Together, these findings clarify the complementary strengths of experimental and computational classification approaches and provide a path to less biased and more equitable variant interpretation in clinical genomics, helping to mitigate disparities in diagnosis across ancestries.

title: The average individual genome: a survey of nearly 1 million whole-genome sequences
abstract: Abstract Background As whole-genome sequencing (WGS) is increasingly used in clinical and public health contexts, clearer expectations regarding the amount of variation present in the “average” human genome are required to contextualise findings. Methods We analysed WGS data from two large population cohorts: 490,541 individuals in UK Biobank (UKB) and 414,830 individuals in All of Us. Following variant and genotype QC, we aimed to assess the range of neutral and disease-associated variation across six genetically-inferred ancestry groups. Results The “average” genome contains ~4.3–5.3 million variants, of which ~1.5% are rare (within-cohort allele frequency < 1%). This includes ~67 autosomal deletions/duplications > 10,000 basepairs per genome, and rare autosomal copy number variants > 1 Mb present in ~ 1 in 41 (2.5%) individuals. On average, ~32–42% of variants per person are homozygous and individuals have ~4 unique runs of homozygosity > 1.5 Mb, with marked variation observed across ancestry groups. Of the ~21– 26,000 SNVs/indels per person in coding exons of MANE Select transcripts, ~48% are predicted to alter the protein, of which ~0.8% are high-confidence loss-of-function and ~0.1% have REVEL score > 0.7 suggestive of pathogenicity. Depending upon parental age, the average genome contains ~63 de novo variants, of which ~75–80% are paternal in origin. Considering only rare variants in GenCC-curated monogenic disease-associated genes, the average genome contains ~1–3 ClinVar pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants, ~2–5 high-confidence loss-of-function variants, and ~50 ClinVar variants of uncertain significance. Most ClinVar pathogenic variants are heterozygous in recessive disease genes, consistent with carrier status, and have multiple ClinVar submitters. Finally, applying polygenic scores (PGS) for 28 common diseases within UKB, we estimate that the average person is in the top 10% for ~3 conditions, and around 1 in 5 people are in the top 1% for at least one PGS. Conclusions The ubiquity of genetic variation in individuals has important implications for policy-makers considering genomic screening and clinicians counselling families. The continued underrepresentation of many global populations reflects a broader limitation of contemporary genomic research, underscoring the need for more inclusive datasets worldwide in order to enable equitable precision medicine.

title: Temporal analysis of clinical variant reclassification (2012–2025)
abstract: ClinVar is the primary archive for human genetic variant classifications, yet existing studies lack a longitudinal perspective of its evolution, often conflating clinical reinterpretation of variant pathogenicity with variant reclassification resulting from database schema evolution. We systematically characterized ClinVar’s 13-year history (2012–2025), analyzing 3.68 million variants across 148 monthly snapshots using both Reference ClinVar (RCV)- and Variation ClinVar (VCV)-formatted Extensible Markup Language (XML) files. An era-stratified heuristic framework was developed to distinguish schema-driven reclassification artifacts from evidence-based clinical reinterpretation. We additionally assessed inter-submitter concordance, disease-domain reclassification patterns, and American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics/Association for Molecular Pathology (ACMG/AMP) evidence documentation. Overall, 9.3% of variants underwent at least one change in aggregate classification category; however, only 0.68% (25,105 variants) ever underwent a medically significant change — that is, a change crossing the clinical actionability boundary between pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) and variant of uncertain significance/benign/likely benign (VUS/B/LB), including 6,340 variants that underwent a drastic pathogenic-to-benign (or vice versa) switch. Accounting for censoring, the cumulative incidence of first reclassification was 2.5% at one year and 15.5% at five years after a variant’s first appearance. We identified three distinct schema eras involving over 120 structural database changes that impact data interpretation, with 2.6% of all reclassification events attributable to the RCV-to-VCV format transition. Reclassification rates were significantly higher in cancer-related genes than in other genes (16.6% vs. 8.2%) and in higher- than in lower-prevalence Mendelian disease variants (19.7% vs. 9.2%). Among multi-submitter variants, 72.1% were concordant while 17.6% maintained conflicting interpretations. Of 697,698 reclassification events, 33.2% resulted from submitter reinterpretation and 18.3% from new-submitter-driven category shifts. Population-frequency releases (the Exome Aggregation Consortium [ExAC] and the Genome Aggregation Database [gnomAD]) and functional evidence from high-throughput saturation mutagenesis and targeted biochemical assays were identified as important contributors to reclassification. Our findings support the need for domain-specific variant reassessment intervals and reinforce the importance of diverse population reference datasets and high-throughput functional assays to minimize classification uncertainty. We also published an open-source pipeline and visualization framework to enable reproducible, era-aware temporal analysis of clinical variant reclassification.

title: Dietary restriction remodels the melanoma immune microenvironment and enhances immunotherapy response with spatial association of SELE+ HEVs and NKT-like cells
abstract: Dietary restriction (DR) can influence cancer progression by remodeling the tumor microenvironment (TME), but its immunomodulatory effects and underlying mechanisms in melanoma remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to characterize DR-associated transcriptional and cellular changes in melanoma and determine their relevance to prognosis and immunotherapy response. We integrated bulk transcriptomic, single-cell RNA-seq, spatial transcriptomic, and experimental data to establish and validate a transcriptome-derived dietary restriction score (DRS) that quantifies DR-associated transcriptional programs. The association of DRS with clinical outcomes and immunotherapy response was evaluated across multiple cohorts. Mouse melanoma models were used to assess the effects of DR on tumor growth and anti-PD-1 efficacy. Cellular enrichment, functional states, spatial colocalization, and intercellular communication were analyzed to identify DR-responsive cell populations and their potential interactions within the melanoma TME. A high DRS was associated with favorable prognosis and improved response to immunotherapy in human melanoma. In mouse models, DR suppressed melanoma growth through immune-dependent mechanisms and enhanced the therapeutic efficacy of anti-PD-1 treatment. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses identified cytotoxic natural killer T (NKT)-like cells and SELE⁺ high endothelial venule (HEV) cells as DR-responsive populations enriched in DRS-high tumors. These populations were associated with enhanced anti-tumor immunity and favorable immunotherapy outcomes. Spatial analysis further revealed significant colocalization between NKT-like cells and SELE⁺ HEV cells in DRS-high tumors, whereas this pattern was not observed in DRS-low tumors. Cell-cell communication analysis suggested that SELE⁺ HEV cells may promote NKT-like cell recruitment and activation through ICAM1-ITGAL/ITGB2 signaling. These findings identify a DR-associated immunovascular axis involving SELE⁺ HEV cells and cytotoxic NKT-like cells that may enhance lymphocyte recruitment, activation, and responsiveness to immune checkpoint blockade. The DRS provides a transcriptomic framework for characterizing DR-associated TME remodeling and supports further investigation of dietary restriction as a potential adjunctive strategy for melanoma immunotherapy.

title: Individuals with autism-associated intellectual disability have an increased burden of de novo variants in cis-regulatory elements of glutamatergic neurons
abstract: ABSTRACT To understand the role of non-coding sequence variation in neurodevelopmental disorders, we studied 709,222 de novo variants (DNVs) using the genomes of 20,366 individuals. We found enrichment of DNVs at cis -regulatory elements (CREs) of all somatic cell types, attributable to the deamination of 5-methylcytosine at CG dinucleotide-dense CREs. In neurodivergent individuals with or without intellectual disability (ID), the DNVs were enriched at genes implicated in autism/ID at promoter-proximal CREs of brain cell types specifically. As the properties of the DNVs were not sufficiently distinctive to explain the phenotypic associations, we performed a multivariate category-wide association study (CWAS) that revealed enrichment of DNVs in CREs of glutamatergic neurons in individuals with ID, with a random forest analysis demonstrating an increased burden of these events in these individuals with ID. Our findings are consistent with a model of non-coding variants contributing to the oligogenic heritability of neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Accelerated and comprehensive pediatric cancer profiling using whole-genome sequencing with adaptive sampling
abstract: Abstract Background Timely and comprehensive molecular classification is essential for therapeutic decision-making in pediatric oncology, yet current diagnostic workflows rely on multi-step, time- and resource-intensive testing strategies. We present a standardized whole-genome sequencing approach with adaptive sampling (AS-WGS) using Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) optimized for pediatric cancers, that enables rapid and comprehensive molecular profiling in a single assay. Methods We designed an AS-WGS panel comprising 380 clinically relevant loci that we applied to the sequencing of 36 pediatric cancer and control samples. To support real-time interpretation, we developed an open-source bioinformatic pipeline (nf-core-oncoseq) enabling on-the-fly analysis during sequencing. We compared the AS-WGS results to those obtained by standard clinical assays, including exome and transcriptome sequencing. Results AS-WGS achieved somatic-grade coverage (mean 172X) in target regions while maintaining pan-genomic coverage (18X), thus supporting genome-wide copy number and methylation analyses. AS-WGS reliably detected all classes of clinically actionable alterations including fusion genes (20/20), small variants (SNVs and indels, in 58/59 mutated genes) and large CNVs (20/21). SNVs were robustly captured down to a 5% allelic frequency, similar to clinical exome sequencing. The PCR-free workflow supported methylation-based tumor classification, providing orthogonal confirmation of hematological and solid tumor subtypes in 9/11 acute lymphoblastic leukemias and in 8/12 solid tumors. All clonal alterations were identified with >5 supporting reads from data generated in the first 24 hours of sequencing (20/20 fusions and 47/47 SNVs with allelic frequencies > 25%), with some, such as large CNVs and methylation predictions, detected within the first hour. Conclusions Our results show that applying AS-WGS to pediatric hematological and solid tumors supports the rapid identification of all classes of genomic alterations and enables methylation-based classification in a single assay. Future efforts aimed at clinical translation will establish its position within the current multi-assay diagnostic landscape.

title: Spatial transcriptomics landscape of livers from patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) progression involves heterogeneous responses and coordinated interactions among parenchymal and nonparenchymal cells. Single-cell transcriptomics has advanced our understanding of cellular heterogeneity, while spatial omics maps molecular signatures within tissue architecture, enabling inference of cell–cell and ligand–receptor interactions, particularly those involving macrophages in MASH. Here, we aimed to characterize spatially resolved transcriptomic alterations in hepatocyte-, hepatic stellate cell (HSC)-, and immune cell-enriched regions in individuals with obesity. We further sought to validate these signatures using public single-cell level RNA sequencing datasets and protein analyses and assess their clinical associations and changes following bariatric surgery. We performed spatial transcriptomic profiling of human liver tissues using the GeoMx Digital Spatial Profiler in 16 patients with MASH across fibrosis stages and eight NonMASH controls. Regions of interest (ROIs) enriched for hepatocytes, immune cells, and HSCs were defined by immunofluorescence-guided pathological annotation. In addition to various bioinformatic analyses on spatial transcriptomic data, we integrated our data with several other public datasets. Finally, the study findings were further validated at the protein level. Each hepatic ROI exhibited distinct molecular alterations during MASH progression. Cytochrome P450 genes were significantly downregulated in hepatocyte-, HSC- and immune cell-enriched ROIs, and negatively correlated with the expression of nuclear receptor and pro-inflammatory genes. With advanced fibrosis in MASH, nonparenchymal ROIs showed marked mitochondrial dysfunction. Ligand‒receptor analysis revealed disrupted inter-regional communication (e.g. loss of protective signals and enhanced pro-fibrotic interactions). Notably, IL32 was consistently upregulated across all three ROI types in MASH versus NonMASH. In addition to validation using public single-cell level datasets, we identified 19 MASH-associated genes, whose expression was correlated with clinical and histologic parameters and reversed following bariatric surgery. Among the key genes identified in our analysis, we selectively validated the hepatic expression of CYP1A2, IL32, and S100A8/9 at the protein level in patients with MASH. Our results reveal compartment-specific metabolic and inflammatory reprogramming in human MASH, highlighting CYP450 suppression, immune activation, disrupted intercellular signaling, and reversibility after bariatric surgery, thereby providing therapeutic implications.

title: Diet-induced programmable GLP-1 delivery by synthetic bacteria enhances anti-obesity efficacy with reduced gut bacterial taxa harboring GLP-1 inactivation potential
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) is an incretin hormone that controls energy homeostasis, and impaired GLP-1 secretion or responsiveness is associated with metabolic diseases. Much effort has been made to develop long-lasting GLP-1-based therapeutics, whereas frequently associated with drug resistance and side effects. GLP-1 is predominantly released postprandially by enteroendocrine cells, while programmable GLP-1 delivery is rarely explored. Herein, genetically engineered probiotic bacteria for diet-induced programmable GLP-1 delivery were developed. The therapeutic efficacy of diet-induced and constitutive GLP-1 delivery was compared in a murine model of obesity, followed by microbiome profiling and functional characterization of gut bacterial GLP-1-degrading enzymes. In murine model of obesity, the anti-adiposity and anti-steatosis effects of diet-induced programmable GLP-1 delivery by synthetic bacteria were greater than that of microbial persistent GLP-1 delivery. Notably, genes encoding microbe-derived GLP-1 peptidase isoenzymes were discovered in gut bacteria specifically enriched by persistent GLP-1 delivery in murine and clinical studies, while diet-induced GLP-1 delivery minimized the abundance of these gut bacteria with GLP-1 inactivation potential. Our findings provide insights into host-microbiome-therapeutic interactions, and highlight programmable delivery strategies for peptide-based therapeutics.

title: Clinico-genomic determinants of relapse in metachronous colorectal cancer metastases
abstract: Abstract Background Given the growing use of cancer screening, colorectal tumors are increasingly diagnosed before metastasizing to distant organs. However, up to 25% of patients with early-stage colorectal cancer later develop metachronous metastases – often years after primary tumor resection. When limited to the liver, they remain potentially curable by surgery, but outcomes following curative-intent resection vary substantially: some patients remain durably disease-free, whereas others relapse within months. Clinico-genomic determinants of this heterogeneity are not well understood, and genomic markers to personalize surgical decisions in patients with metachronous liver metastases are lacking. Methods We assembled a deeply annotated cohort of 41 colorectal cancer patients undergoing resection of metachronous liver metastases – with whole-exome and transcriptome sequencing of metastases and matched primary tumors (where available) and structured annotations of their longitudinal clinical trajectories, including a median follow-up of 66.4 months, relapse after metastatic surgery, adjuvant therapies, radiologic assessments, and blood-based markers. We further dissected relapse-associated genomic features in five independent datasets. Results Early relapse (< 12 months) correlated with a larger number of metachronous liver metastases and a characteristic copy-number pattern involving loss of arms 3p and 5q. Metastases with late/no relapse were characterized by multi-hit APC mutations. These genomic features also correlated with significant differences in relapse-free survival after metastatic surgery, and they were consistent between patients with and without adjuvant therapy for their primary and metastatic tumors. Early-relapsing metastases typically harbored an accumulation of multiple relapse-associated genomic changes. Moreover, metachronous metastases differed in genomic characteristics from synchronous metastases in an independent cohort, exhibiting a higher frequency of 5q loss and a higher burden of copy-number alterations relative to their matched primaries, suggesting continued evolution after primary-tumor resection. Transcriptomically, relapse-associated copy-number changes correlated with gene-dosage effects on the respective arms and differential expression of genes related to proliferation and metabolism. They also correlated with advanced disease and shorter survival in two independent datasets. Conclusions Our study characterizes the clinico-genomic basis of early relapse in metachronous liver metastases. Ultimately, these features could help identify patients with a high propensity to relapse after surgery and personalize the management of colorectal cancer patients with metachronous liver metastases.

title: Recessive variants in ESCRT-II component VPS25 alter vesicular transport and small extracellular vesicle processing in lethal neonatal encephalopathy
abstract: Abstract Background The role of small extracellular vesicles (sEVs), such as exosomes, in cell-to-cell communication is increasingly recognized. Both during development and postnatally, sEVs have been shown to mediate a multitude of essential functions in the central nervous system. While abnormal sEV biogenesis has been observed in a number of neurodevelopmental disorders, a causal link has been largely lacking. Methods We clinically evaluated five families in which newborns presented with a novel neonatal-onset encephalopathy. Positional mapping, exome sequencing, and trio exome sequencing were utilized to identify the underlying genetic variants. Additionally, we utilized Vps25 hypomorphic mouse mutants and performed cellular assays to evaluate ESCRT-II interaction, cellular localization, and sEV secretion and cargo capacities. Results The observed lethal encephalopathy is characterized by severe hypotonia, brain anomalies, and epilepsy. In families 1, 4, and 5 (multiplex consanguineous), we identified a novel homozygous missense variant in VPS25 as the likely candidate. Family 2 comprises a simplex case with two missense variants in trans in VPS25 , one of which impacts the same residue as in the other three families. Family 3 also comprises a simplex case where we revealed a homozygous missense variant. VPS25 is an essential component of ESCRT-II, itself required for sEV biogenesis. We show that Vps25 hypomorphic mouse mutants recapitulate the developmental brain malformation observed in patients. We also show that mutant VPS25 is associated with abnormal ESCRT-II interaction, abnormal cellular localization, and highly abnormal sEVs. Specifically, mutant cells displayed engorged multivesicular bodies and were significantly defective in their capacity to secrete sEVs such as exosomes, while secreted sEVs contained altered cargo, lacking vital proteins for axon protection and maintenance. Conclusions We report a novel neurodevelopmental disorder caused by biallelic hypomorphic variants in VPS25 . The consistent impact of these variants on sEV biogenesis suggests a potential pathomechanism. While future cases will further delineate the phenotypic spectrum, these findings offer a new perspective on abnormal sEVs as drivers of human neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Comprehensive adjudication identifies 108 high-confidence genetic signals for Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias
abstract: Background: The Alzheimer's Disease Sequencing Project Gene Verification Committee developed a systematic framework to adjudicate genetic evidence for AD and related dementias, addressing wide variation in association quality. Methods: Phase 1 established tiered criteria by evaluating 23 nominated loci across study designs. Phase 2 applied this framework to 29 large-scale genome-wide studies published since 2015, tiering 163 unique loci. Results: Phase 1 yielded 17 high-confidence loci (12 linked to specific genes), and Phase 2 identified 111 high-confidence loci/genes with replicated associations across ancestries and convergent single-variant/variant-set evidence. Prioritized loci highlight APP processing, microglial immunity, and lipid metabolism pathways, including genes not captured by existing resources like Agora or Open Targets. Summarized results can be viewed at https://topgenes.niagads.org/. Conclusion: This rigorously adjudicated catalog represents the most comprehensive AD/ADRD genetics resource to date, providing a foundation for functional validation and therapeutic discovery with broad applicability to complex diseases.

title: Ciprofloxacin resistance in Klebsiella pneumoniae: phenotype prediction from genotype and global distribution of resistance determinants
authors: Emília Ma. M. de Andrade Belitardo
on behalf of the KlebNET-GSP AMR Genotype-Phenotype Group
abstract: Abstract Background Ciprofloxacin resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae is common or emerging in many geographies, and knowledge of local resistance rates is important for empirical therapy. While K. pneumoniae ciprofloxacin resistance determinants are known, there is a lack of systematic data on the effect of these determinants, alone and in combination, and there are no publicly accessible tools for predicting ciprofloxacin resistance from whole genome sequence data. Methods The KlebNET-GSP AMR Genotype-Phenotype Group aggregated a matched genotype-phenotype dataset of n = 12,167 K. pneumoniae species complex ( Kp SC) isolates from 27 countries between 2001 and 2021. We developed a rule-based classifier to predict ciprofloxacin resistance by categorizing the number of mutations in the quinolone resistance determining regions of gyrA and parC and the number of plasmid-mediated quinolone resistance genes, including the presence/absence of aac(6 ' )-Ib-cr (which can acetylate ciprofloxacin). Predictive performance was assessed using the discovery dataset, with the reassessment of discrepant and concordant isolates; and validated using externally contributed datasets ( n = 7,030 Kp SC isolates). Results The rule-based classifier predicted R vs S/I with categorical agreement, sensitivity, and specificity > 96%, and major/very major error rates < 4%. Performance was similar across diverse Kp SC sources (human, animal, other), species, and intra-species lineages. External validation of the classifier yielded overall 90.18% categorical agreement [95% confidence interval (CI), 89.49–90.88%], 8.74% major errors [95% CI, 7.41–10.06%], 4.19% very major errors [95% CI, 3.60–4.77%], and 10.14% minor errors [95% CI, 9.44–10.85%]. We implemented the classifier in Kleborate, a command-line tool that is integrated into the Pathogenwatch web platform. Using this to assess the global distribution of ciprofloxacin resistance determinants in Kp SC genomes available in Pathogenwatch ( n = 31,319, from 109 countries between years 2000–2023), we observed a significant positive association between national quinolone consumption rates and predicted ciprofloxacin resistance (R 2 = 0.20, p = 0.004). Conclusion Ciprofloxacin resistance phenotypes can be reasonably predicted from genotype, which is sufficient for informing surveillance. However, unexplained resistance remains and accuracy is insufficient for clinical applications. We demonstrate the value of aggregating genotype-phenotype data to explore resistance mechanisms and develop predictors, but highlight complexities in combining phenotype data from different assays and standards.

title: Resolving disease causality by integrating polygenic risk into propensity score matching
abstract: Disentangling causal relationships between diseases from associations driven by shared genetic and environmental risk remains a major challenge. We developed PRIMA (polygenic risk–integrated matching approach), a framework that incorporates exposure-specific polygenic risk scores and clinical covariates into propensity score matching. We evaluated PRIMA using liability-threshold simulations and disease-pair analyses in 333,370 unrelated UK Biobank participants of European ancestry, and compared its estimates with clinical matching, Mendelian randomization and survival analyses. In simulations, PRIMA reduced bias due to shared genetic liability and recovered effect estimates closer to the expected causal effects than clinical matching alone, while remaining sensitive to unmeasured confounding. In UK Biobank analyses, integrating polygenic risk improved genetic and clinical balance and materially altered association estimates for a subset of disease pairs. PRIMA identified additional associations not detected by Mendelian randomization and showed greater concordance with survival analyses. PRIMA provides a scalable framework for incorporating polygenic liability into observational disease-pair analyses. It complements existing causal inference methods, although causal interpretation remains conditional on appropriate model specification, sufficient overlap and adequate control of confounding.

title: Evaluating gene expression-based approaches for functional assessment of non-coding variants in neurodevelopmental disorders
abstract: Non-coding variants associated with neurodevelopmental disorders are difficult to interpret because their regulatory effects are subtle and depend on locus- and stage-specific epigenetic contexts. Transcriptional mis-regulation of nearby genes is the most reliable sign of functional relevance. RNA-seq studies usually detect this via differential gene expression (DEG) analysis, which requires healthy controls and typically more than twofold expression changes. Allele-specific expression (ASE) analysis, may detect subtler effects by directly comparing expression of alleles on the intact and the affected chromosomes within the same sample. We evaluated ASE power using real RNA-seq data, in silico simulations, and a clinical case. We combined transcriptome profiling of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and neural progenitor cells (NPCs) with in silico modeling of gene-expression changes to estimate statistical power. We compared two strategies: DEG between variant carriers and non-carriers, and ASE within heterozygous individuals. For clinical validation, we used CRISPR-Cas9 base editing to introduce a synonymous single-nucleotide variant (SNV) adjacent to the candidate regulatory variant in patient-derived NPCs and performed targeted RNA-seq. Simulations and empirical data showed that DEG has higher power for most genes, even with substantial inter-individual or biological variability. ASE surpassed DEG only for genes containing heterozygous SNVs and sequenced at high depth. In a patient carrying a translocation breakpoint near AUTS2 , we generated iPSC and NPC lines with SNV-labeled AUTS2 alleles and devised an inexpensive target-enrichment assay for high-sensitivity ASE profiling, but neither approach detected gene misregulation consistent with the phenotype under current biological models. Our results suggested that DEG and ASE assays are complementary rather than competing strategies. We also demonstrate a practical path to sensitive ASE detection, both in whole-transcriptome and targeted RNA-sequencing, using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated allele labeling. This framework helps researchers to choose cost-effective transcriptomic designs for the functional validation of non-coding variants implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Germline pathogenic variants identification through comprehensive cancer genome profiling
abstract: Abstract Background: Comprehensive cancer genome profiling (CGP) is recommended for the identification of actionable somatic mutations in a selected subgroup of cancer patients. Some variants detected by CGP can be constitutional. The aim of this study is to evaluate the rate of potential and confirmed constitutional pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants (overall defined as PVs) identified through CGP according to the recommendations of the European Society of Medical Oncology Methods: This is a prospective interventional trial enrolling solid cancer patients in whom molecular assessment was clinically indicated based on national guidelines, referring them for CGP. Patients with suspected constitutional variants were subsequently referred for germline testing. The present analysis focuses on the first two years of the program, from January 2022 to December 2023. Results: Of 2688 samples (2674 patients) with a CGP report, more than half were represented by female reproductive system cancers. 16% of the patients were addressed to genetic evaluation for 527 suspected constitutional PVs, with a compliance to genetic counselling of 80%. 331 patients underwent germline testing, of whom 73% harbored at least one PV, with 66% of tested variants confirmed to be germline. Interestingly, 16% of germline variants were secondary findings and 20% of the confirmed “on-tumor” germline PVs were in moderate-risk genes. Eighteen additional constitutional PVs were identified in 17 patients based on the results of other somatic tests or through additional tests requested following genetic counselling (0.6% of the entire cohort). Conclusions: Constitutional PVs were detected in about 10% of an unselected solid tumor cohort through CGP. A relevant fraction of the constitutional PVs were secondary findings or constitutional variants in moderate penetrance genes, that would not have been detected based on current guidelines. The integration of CGP with systematic genetic counseling provides a comprehensive approach that optimizes both therapeutic decision-making and hereditary cancer prevention. Trial Registration: Protocol ID: FPG500, ID number: 3837, ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06020625.

title: Using SpliceAI to triage splice-altering variants in 7,220 individuals with rare conditions highlights limitations of the precomputed scores
abstract: Abstract Background SpliceAI is a deep learning algorithm that predicts whether genetic variants are likely to affect splicing. Precomputed SpliceAI predictions for all theoretical SNVs and small indels were released in 2019, and are used by variant annotation tools such as VEP and dbNSFP to batch annotate large numbers of variants quickly. While the use of precomputed scores vastly reduces the computational cost of retrieving SpliceAI predictions, several limitations to their utility have emerged, for which the impact on the prioritisation of likely splice-altering variants in cohort studies has not been established.
